newsitem.title: USA: Hilton seeks to bar ITT's hotel sale to FelCor.
newsitem.headline: Hilton seeks to bar ITT's hotel sale to FelCor.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp. Thursday launched an aggressive legal attack on takeover target ITT Corp. seeking to bar ITT's proposed $200 million sale of five hotels to FelCor Suite Hotels Inc.

In amending a previously filed suit, Beverly Hills-based Hilton also asked a federal court to prevent ITT from selling any more assets without first holding an open auction and seeking shareholder approval.

Its suit claims ITT, which is the subject of a $6.5 billion hostile bid by Hilton, has abandoned its strategy to focus on core assets and is engaged in a plan to break-up ITT. It argues the FelCor sale, as well as talks to sell other upscale hotels, reflect ITT's new tactics.

In a sharply written news release, Hilton said the moves indicate a "scorched earth" policy, adding a "change in control" provision of the FelCor sale shows ITT's management "is destroying a valuable corporate asset."
A spokesman for New York-based ITT declined to comment directly on the amended complaint because ITT had yet to be served with it, however, he staunchly defended the proposed sale to FelCor.
"Everything we have done has been done with the goal of building value for our shareholders," ITT's Jim Gallagher said.
Executives for Dallas-based FelCor were not immediately available to comment.

The filing in U.S. District Court in Las Vegas amends a previous complaint that sought to dismantle the company's shareholder rights plan, or so-called "poison pill," that is a common defence used to thwart hostile takeovers.

Hilton launched its $55-per-share takeover bid for ITT in late January, and ITT later rejected the offer as inadequate. ITT then began selling assets to focus on core businesses in hotels and gambling. ITT owns Sheraton hotels and Caesars casinos.

On Monday, ITT signed a definitive agreement to sell the hotels to FelCor. Under the deal, ITT Sheraton would still manage the hotels but if ITT is taken over in a hostile deal, FelCor retains the right to terminate the management contract.
Hilton claims the provision decreases the hotels' value, but ITT says it is standard procedure in these deals.

The FelCor sale, plus talks that could lead to the sale of the upscale St. Regis hotel in New York and the Phoenician in Scottsdale, Arizona, also has Hilton concerned that ITT is selling core assets.

Such a tactic would depart from ITT's stated strategy, and would directly conflict with Hilton's reasons for acquiring ITT. Hilton wants to own major, high-end hotel properties and be a leader in the hotel and gambling industries.
In the past, ITT has said the FelCor hotels were not part of its core holdings, and it has declined to comment on the possible sale of the St. Regis and Phoenician.
The takeover battle has exploded into a war of words between the two sides, financial analysts and market experts concede.

"What Hilton wants the world to believe is that ITT is dismantling the company," said Jim Murren, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, "What I believe ITT is doing is selling assets at extraordinarily high valuations in a sellers market."

Indeed, Gallagher noted FelCor paid ITT about 12.5 times cash flow for the hotels, whereas Hilton's offer for the entire company represents is valued at about nine times cash flow. Hilton has said it is willing to pay a higher price if ITT would only meet with its management to discuss a merger.
Analysts said, however, that the change of control provision was uncommon, though several conceded it has been used more often in recent years.
In this case "clearly it's a poison pill kind of thing," said Marvin Roffman of Roffman, Miller Associates. "To me, it was done intentionally to prevent a takeover."
Meanwhile, shareholders reacted positively to the latest sparring, bidding Hilton shares up $1.875 to $28.50 on the New York Stock Exchange and sending ITT's shares 87.5 cents higher to $59.50.
